_about: Clone reports seeded on Clone Report. Every entry is a publicly documented case: a lawsuit or court ruling, a store takedown, or a public statement by the original game's developer, with links to press coverage in `sources`. Notes describe what was claimed and what happened, not a finding by Clone Report. Steam ids were checked against SteamSpy in Nov 2026. Loaded automatically on server start; each `key` is added once, so a report an admin later edits, rejects or deletes is left alone. Set SEED_REPORTS=0 to skip.

reports.notes: In 2012 a US federal court (District of New Jersey) ruled in Tetris Holding v. Xio Interactive that Mino copied the look of Tetris, including its board, piece shapes and screen layout, and granted summary judgment to The Tetris Company. The case is often cited as the first US ruling that a game clone infringed copyright.

Spry Fox sued 6waves Lolapps in 2012, saying Yeti Town copied Triple Town after 6waves had seen the game in confidential talks about publishing it. The case settled in October 2012: Spry Fox took ownership of the Yeti Town IP and the game left the App Store.

Bethesda sued Warner Bros. and Behaviour Interactive in 2018, claiming the Westworld mobile game copied Fallout Shelter's design and reused its code (Behaviour had co-developed Fallout Shelter). The companies settled at the turn of 2019 and the Westworld game was shut down.

In May 2020 Ubisoft sued Apple and Google in a US federal court for distributing Area F2, which Ubisoft's complaint described as a near carbon copy of Rainbow Six Siege, from its operator selection screen to its maps and scoring.
PUBG Corp. sued NetEase in a US federal court in 2018, claiming Rules of Survival and Knives Out copied PUBG's look, items and gameplay. The companies settled in 2019.

PUBG Corp. sued NetEase in 2018, claiming Knives Out and Rules of Survival copied PUBG; that case settled in 2019. Krafton, PUBG's parent company, later brought another copyright case over Knives Out, which was settled in December 2023.

In January 2022 Krafton, PUBG's publisher, sued Garena in a US federal court, claiming Free Fire and Free Fire Max copied many elements of PUBG. The suit also named Apple and Google for distributing the games. This report does not cover how the case ended.

Blizzard and Valve sued uCool and Lilith Games in a US federal court in September 2015, claiming their mobile games copied characters and art from Dota 2 and Blizzard games. In 2018 the court let the claims against Heroes Charge go forward; Blizzard and Valve later dropped them, which was widely read as a private settlement.

Riot Games sued Moonton in 2017 and again in 2022, claiming Mobile Legends copied League of Legends and League of Legends: Wild Rift. Both US cases were dismissed on the grounds that another country's courts were better placed to hear them. The companies signed a global settlement in April 2024 and Riot withdrew its lawsuits.

In November 2019 the Pudong New Area People's Court in Shanghai ruled that 4399 Network's Clash of Fighters and Gunplay Battlefront infringed the copyright of Overwatch and awarded Blizzard and NetEase 4 million yuan (about $570,000). The original Overwatch has since been replaced by Overwatch 2.

In November 2019 the Pudong New Area People's Court in Shanghai ruled that 4399 Network's Gunplay Battlefront and Clash of Fighters infringed the copyright of Overwatch and awarded Blizzard and NetEase 4 million yuan (about $570,000). The original Overwatch has since been replaced by Overwatch 2.

The Pokémon Company sued the companies behind Pocket Monster Reissue in China in December 2021. In September 2024 it announced that the Shenzhen Intermediate People's Court had found the game copied Pokémon characters and creatures, including Ash and Pikachu, and ordered 107 million yuan (about $15 million) in damages. Some defendants appealed.
Electronic Arts sued Zynga in August 2012, claiming The Ville copied the design, look and features of The Sims Social. The companies settled out of court in February 2013.

Vlambeer said Ninja Fishing copied the design of Radical Fishing, its 2010 web game, while Vlambeer was still making the mobile version, Ridiculous Fishing (released 2013). Vlambeer wrote an open letter to Gamenauts and later said the episode nearly ended the studio. Gamenauts responded publicly at the time.

1024 came out weeks after Threes! with the same sliding, number-merging grid. The Threes! team published a long post in March 2014 about the copies that followed their game, naming 1024 among them. Press at the time described 1024 and 2048 as copies of Threes!.

2048 was released as a free web game weeks after Threes!. Its creator said it was based on 1024, itself a copy of Threes!. The Threes! team spoke out publicly about 2048 and the other copies, and press widely described 2048 as a Threes! knockoff.

When Zynga released Dream Heights in January 2012, NimbleBit published an open letter sarcastically 'congratulating' Zynga, with side-by-side images comparing it to Tiny Tower, which Apple had named its iPhone game of the year.

reports.original_developer: Josh Wardle (now The New York Times)
reports.notes: In January 2022 Apple removed Wordle - The App and other paid copies of Wordle from the App Store after a public backlash. The app's creator later apologized and said he had crossed a line.

Witch Beam called Unpacking Master a near 1:1 imitation of Unpacking. The game briefly topped the App Store download charts in January 2022 and was then removed from the App Store and Google Play. SayGames said it had underestimated how similar the two games were.

Atari, which held the home console rights to Pac-Man, sued Philips. In 1982 the US Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit found K.C. Munchkin! substantially similar to Pac-Man and ordered a preliminary injunction that took the game off store shelves.

Palworld has been widely compared to Pokémon in the press since its 2024 launch. In September 2024 Nintendo and The Pokémon Company sued Pocketpair in Tokyo for patent infringement over game mechanics such as throwing a ball to catch creatures. The suit is about patents, not copied characters, and was still unresolved as of 2026.
In December 2017 a paid app called Cuphead appeared on the App Store using the game's name and art. Studio MDHR said it had nothing to do with the app, and Apple removed it.
Mob Wars creator David Maestri sued Zynga in February 2009, claiming Mafia Wars copied his game. The case settled later in 2009; TechCrunch reported a payment in the high seven figures.

Reviewers at the time called The Great Giana Sisters a rip-off of Super Mario Bros., and its UK box read 'The Brothers are History!'. It was pulled from sale in 1988 after Nintendo sent Rainbow Arts a letter about the similarities. Accounts differ on whether there was a formal settlement.

Hole.io topped the App Store in June 2018, months before Donut County, a game about a hole that swallows a town, came out. Donut County's developer Ben Esposito publicly called it out as a clone of his unreleased game, while noting there were differences, and the case was widely covered as an example of mobile publishers copying indie games.

Hasbro sued the makers of Scrabulous in July 2008, claiming the Facebook game infringed its Scrabble copyrights and trademarks. Scrabulous was disabled for US and Canadian Facebook users days later. A Delhi court then ruled that the game's name infringed the Scrabble trademark but the gameplay itself could not be protected, and the game came back as Lexulous. Hasbro withdrew its US suit in December 2008.

Artic International sold circuit-board kits that turned arcade cabinets into Defense Command, a game virtually identical to Williams' Defender. In 1982 the US Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit upheld an injunction against Artic, a ruling that confirmed arcade game programs and their screens are protected by copyright.

Omni Video Games sold arcade machines called Scramble 2 that copied Konami's Scramble. In Stern Electronics v. Kaufman (1982) the US Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit held that a game's sounds and images are protected as an audiovisual work and that Omni's game infringed.

NCSoft sued Webzen in 2021, saying R2M copied Lineage M. A Seoul court ruled for NCSoft in August 2023, and in 2025 the Seoul High Court ordered Webzen to pay about 16.9 billion won (roughly $12 million) and to stop offering R2M, finding the similarities amounted to unfair competition. Webzen said it would appeal.

Steam removed Myth of Empires in December 2021 after Studio Wildcard and its parent company Snail Games claimed it was built on stolen ARK: Survival Evolved source code, pointing to hundreds of matching code names and near-identical mechanics. Angela Game denied it. The companies settled in October 2023: Angela Game acknowledged harming Snail's business, and Snail agreed to help re-release the game as a partner.

Pickmos was widely criticized in April 2026 for looking like Palworld and Pokémon, with creatures resembling Pikachu and Lucario and models compared to Zelda and Overwatch. Its publisher Networkgo pulled the Steam page, saying it had stepped in to supervise development and revise the game. The page returned in May 2026 with replaced art.

In January 2024 a game called The Suika Game appeared on the PlayStation Store. Aladdin X, the maker of Suika Game, said it had absolutely nothing to do with it. Aladdin X had already warned players about lookalike Suika Game apps on mobile stores in 2023.

Sony sued Tencent in July 2025, calling Light of Motiram a slavish clone of its Horizon games and pointing to the setting, a red-haired heroine, robot animals and the marketing. The case was settled confidentially in December 2025 and dismissed, and Light of Motiram was taken off Steam and the Epic Games Store.

reports.clone_name: Mini Subway: Logic on the Metro Line
reports.notes: Mini Subway: Logic on the Metro Line launched on the Switch eShop in July 2022 and was widely reported as a copy of Mini Metro. Dinosaur Polo Club said it would take legal action if needed, and the game was removed from the eShop in early August 2022.

reports.clone_name: My Lost Kitty in Big City Town
reports.notes: In July 2024 Double Dagger Studio publicly pointed out mobile copies of Little Kitty, Big City, including My Lost Kitty in Big City Town and My Little Cat Lost in Big City, as part of a wider complaint by indie developers about app stores not removing knockoffs.

Lilith Games sued uCool in 2015, claiming Heroes Charge cloned its Chinese mobile game Soul Clash, released in February 2014, six months before Heroes Charge. Blizzard and Valve later sued both companies over characters they said came from their games (see the Heroes Charge vs Dota 2 report).

Konami sued Roxor Games in 2005 over In the Groove, a dance game that could be installed into Dance Dance Revolution arcade cabinets, claiming patent and trademark infringement. The case settled in 2006: Konami took over the In the Groove intellectual property and Roxor agreed to respect Konami's rights.

Zynga sued Brazilian developer Vostu in June 2011, claiming MegaCity and other Vostu games copied CityVille and other Zynga games. The case settled in December 2011: Vostu paid Zynga an undisclosed sum and agreed to change four of its games.

Blizzard and its Chinese partner NetEase sued the makers of Crouching Dragon Legends (also reported as Legend of the Hidden Dragon). In 2014 the Shanghai No. 1 Intermediate People's Court ordered the game's makers to stop operating it and to pay damages; reports differ on the amount.
Blizzard and NetEase filed a lawsuit in August 2019 claiming the mobile game Glorious Saga copied World of Warcraft. The game went offline at the end of that month, shortly after the suit was filed.

reports.clone_name: The Last Hope - Dead Zone Survival
reports.clone_developer: Virtual Global Games (publisher: West Connection Limited)
reports.original_name: The Last of Us Part I
reports.notes: Press described this eShop game as a Last of Us rip-off. In 2023 its trailer was blocked by a copyright claim from Sony Interactive Entertainment, and the game was then no longer available on the UK and US eShops.

Steelkrill, the developer of The Backrooms 1998, said this game was "an exact 1:1 copy" of theirs released under another name with an AI-made cover. After Steelkrill's DMCA requests, PlayStation and Xbox removed it; it was still on the Switch eShop in February 2025.
This game appeared on the Switch eShop in April 2026 using the Hytale name. Hypixel Studios said it was not theirs and that its legal team was taking action against it.
Panik Arcade publicly warned players that COIN PIT, an eShop game from the same publisher as the Hytale knock-off, imitated CloverPit. Press reported that the listing was later removed.
In December 2025 Panik Arcade warned that an eShop game using the CloverPit name "is NOT MADE BY US". CloverPit itself was not on Switch at the time.

Press described this PS4 game as a rip-off of Grand Theft Auto: Vice City. It was released on the PlayStation Store in August 2024 and pulled after a complaint from Take-Two, Rockstar's parent company.

Tencent sued over maps in Crisis Action that it said copied CrossFire's. A Shenzhen court ruled for Tencent in 2019, and the Guangdong High People's Court upheld it in December 2021 in what was reported as China's first game-map copyright case, with damages of more than 25 million yuan.

NetEase, Minecraft's operator in China, sued the makers of Mini World in 2019. In November 2022 the Guangdong High People's Court found the two games nearly indistinguishable and ruled it unfair competition, ordering 50 million yuan in damages and an injunction.

Crazy Kong kept Donkey Kong's gameplay with redrawn graphics. It was licensed for operation only in Japan; Nintendo revoked the license in 1982 after cabinets were exported. The dispute reached a US court in Nintendo v. Elcon (E.D. Mich., 1982).

Magnavox sued Atari, saying Pong was based on the table tennis game of the Magnavox Odyssey, which Atari founder Nolan Bushnell had played at a demonstration before Pong was made. This was a patent case; Atari settled in 1976 by taking a license from Magnavox.

Midway, which held the US rights to Pac-Man, sued sellers of conversion kits for Mighty Mouth. In Midway v. Dirkschneider (D. Neb. 1981) the court described the game as nearly identical to Pac-Man and granted Midway a preliminary injunction.

Midway, which held the US rights to Galaxian, sued sellers of Galactic Invader conversion kits. In Midway v. Dirkschneider (D. Neb. 1981) the court described the game as nearly identical to Galaxian and granted a preliminary injunction.
Kamikaze III was one of the conversion kits in Midway v. Dirkschneider (D. Neb. 1981). The court described it as nearly identical to Galaxian and granted Midway a preliminary injunction.
Press flagged this eShop game in April 2025 as a scam copy riding on the viral co-op horror game R.E.P.O., which was not on Switch.
Press warned in January 2025 that this eShop game imitated the name and look of Black Myth: Wukong, which was not released on Switch.
Landfall said the Switch games using the Content Warning name were unofficial and that it was working to get them removed.
Press described Palland, released on the Switch eShop in July 2025, as a rip-off of Palworld, which was not on Switch.
Press described this eShop game, released in November 2024, as a rip-off of the Steam hit TCG Card Shop Simulator.
Press described this eShop game, released in May 2026, as a knock-off borrowing the names and look of Gears of War and Dead Space.
In May 2026 Google Play listings used the name of Nintendo's Tomodachi Life: Living the Dream, which is only on Switch. Press reported the clones, and a listing was later removed.

In June 2024 kindanice, the creator of Dire Decks, said Terry Brash had copied the game and was releasing it on Steam under another name. Brash called Wildcard a "rewrite" and "clone" of Dire Decks and said: "I liked the game, so I made a clone with extra stuff."
In July 2024 Kenney, the developer of MakeRoom, asked the developer of Flora Corner not to copy the game. Hacktic apologised and said it would change the game's art.
In January 2026 Lazy Flock, the studio behind Haunted Paws, said Ghostly Whiskers on the PlayStation Store "IS A DIRECT COPY" of their unreleased game, made with AI-generated assets.
Press described this PlayStation Store game, listed in January 2025, as a close imitation of Animal Crossing: New Horizons. The listing was later removed.

In March 2026 fans found an App Store game called Peak!. Aggro Crab said: "It's fake, but they take FOREVER to get removed" and that the studio has no plans for mobile; Landfall said "It is not real."

In August 2025 a PlayStation Store listing called Peaked Climbing, with mostly AI-made screenshots, was flagged to Landfall. Landfall said it had been reporting "a bunch of these AI slop things for the past year".
Aggro Crab, co-developer of PEAK, called Cliff a "microtransaction-riddled Roblox slop ripoff" and said it would rather players pirate PEAK than play it.
Press described this PlayStation Store listing as a near-copy of Gray Zone Warfare, with AI-made cover art, similar icons and a near-identical tagline.

Webzen sued the developer and operator of Qijishenhua in China over copying MU Online. The Pudong New Area People's Court in Shanghai ruled for Webzen and awarded more than 5 million yuan, reported at the time as the highest award in an online game case in China.

reports.clone_name: Legend of Blue Moon (web and 3D mobile versions)
reports.notes: Wemade sued Kingnet in China in 2019 over unlicensed games based on The Legend of Mir 2. In 2021 the Hangzhou Intermediate People's Court ordered both versions of the game to stop service and awarded Wemade 9.2 million yuan in total.
In December 2022 Riot Games sued NetEase in several countries, saying Hyper Front copied VALORANT's maps, characters and weapons. NetEase shut Hyper Front down in April 2023.
An unofficial Lethal Company app was one of the top games on the iOS App Store in February 2024. Zeekerss said the mobile version was "likely a scam of some sort" and not made by them.
In April 2025 PlayStation Store listings used the Schedule I name while the game was PC-only. TVGS said: "these are not affiliated with me in any way." PlayStation removed Schedule 1 Syndicate.
Another PlayStation Store listing that used the Schedule I name in April 2025. TVGS said the listings were "not affiliated with me in any way."

CGI LAB released several eShop games using the Unpacking name in 2024 (also listed as Unpacking: Deluxe Edition). Witch Beam reported them to Nintendo, and creative director Wren Brier called them "egregious scams" that were "purposely tricking Nintendo customers into buying cheap fakes."

Apple removed Temple Jump in February 2012 in a sweep of copycat apps from the same developer. Imangi co-founder Natalia Luckyanova said it "was clearly a scam that traded entirely on the popularity of Temple Run."
One of the lookalike apps Apple removed in February 2012 from the developer behind Temple Jump.
One of the lookalike apps Apple removed in February 2012 from the developer behind Temple Jump.
One of the lookalike apps from the developer behind Temple Jump that Apple removed in February 2012.

An app called Pokemon Yellow, not made by Nintendo or The Pokémon Company, reached No. 2 on the App Store in February 2012 and reportedly crashed on launch. Apple removed it within days, and The Pokémon Company said it would act against unauthorised games.

A second unofficial Pokémon app removed from the App Store in February 2012, alongside the fake Pokemon Yellow. The Pokémon Company said it works against "the unauthorised release of games" that mislead fans.
Vlambeer said SkyFar copied LUFTRAUSERS and got it removed from the App Store in 2013. It was later relisted; Vlambeer's Rami Ismail said of it: "It's not about the game, it's about the money."
The Tetris Company, through its lawyers, sent a takedown request for the falling-block game Tetrada, and in February 2011 it was set to be removed from the Windows Phone Marketplace.
